infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation¶

Allocation-rule computation for the influencer-game router.

Implements the proportional-share allocation rule

\[G_i(\mathbf{x}, b) \;=\; \frac{f_i(x_i, b)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} f_j(x_j, b)}\]

(eqn. 1, Lovett & Fu 2024) and the resulting expected utility

\[u_i(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \sum_{b \in \mathbb{B}} B(b)\, G_i(\mathbf{x}, b)\]

(eqn. 2). The influence kernel is the multivariate Gaussian with a shared covariance \(\Sigma\), preserving the kernel-symmetry assumption of Theorems 1–5.

Note

AGENTS.md §4 rule 2 reserves the canonical reward to infl_ens.inflgame.env. This module computes \(G_i\) and \(u_i\) directly for routing-time convenience; when integrating with the trainer, route position updates through env rather than calling these functions twice.

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.allocation_weights(positions, grid, cov)[source]¶

Allocation matrix \(G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k)\) for every (agent, trait) pair.

Computed in log-space (softmax over agents at each trait) for numerical stability. The returned matrix has columns that sum to one across agents.

Parameters:

  • positions (numpy.ndarray) – Agent positions, shape (N, L).

  • grid (numpy.ndarray) – Trait points, shape (K, L).

  • cov (numpy.ndarray) – Shared MV-Gaussian covariance \(\Sigma\), shape (L, L). For isotropic kernels, pass sigma**2 * np.eye(L).

Returns:

Allocation matrix G with G[i, k] = G_i(x, b_k); G.sum(axis=0) is identically 1. Shape (N, K).

Return type:

numpy.ndarray

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.expected_utilities(positions, grid, weights, cov)[source]¶

Expected utility \(u_i(\mathbf{x})\) per agent.

Implements \(u_i = \sum_k B(b_k)\, G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k)\). Utilities sum to one in expectation because \(\sum_i G_i \equiv 1\) at every trait.

Parameters:

  • positions (numpy.ndarray) – Agent positions, shape (N, L).

  • grid (numpy.ndarray) – Trait points, shape (K, L).

  • weights (numpy.ndarray) – Resource weights \(B(b_k)\), shape (K,), summing to one.

  • cov (numpy.ndarray) – Shared covariance \(\Sigma\), shape (L, L).

Returns:

Utility vector, shape (N,).

Return type:

numpy.ndarray

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.strategic_routing_weights(positions, grid, cov, *, eps=1e-12)[source]¶

Per-trait \(G_i(1 - G_i)\)-weighted routing probabilities.

The strategic gradient of agent \(i\)’s expected utility under the multivariate-Gaussian influencer’s game is

\[\nabla_{x_i} u_i \;=\; \sum_b B(b)\, G_i(\mathbf{x}, b)\,(1 - G_i(\mathbf{x}, b))\, \Sigma^{-1}(b - x_i).\]

The factor \(G_i(1-G_i)\) down-weights traits where agent \(i\) already dominates (large \(G_i\)) and up-weights contested traits (intermediate \(G_i\)). Routing queries according to

\[p_i(\mathbf{x}, b) \;=\; \frac{G_i(\mathbf{x}, b)\,(1 - G_i(\mathbf{x}, b))} {\sum_j G_j(\mathbf{x}, b)\,(1 - G_j(\mathbf{x}, b))}\]

matches the strategic gradient in expectation: an agent’s expected SFT drift becomes \(\propto \nabla_{x_i} u_i\) (up to the constant \(\Sigma^{-1}\) metric and a normalising factor), rather than the naive proportional drift \(\propto \sum_b B(b) G_i (b - x_i)\).

Columns sum to one across agents and the routing reduces to uniform (\(p_i \equiv 1/N\)) at clone-start (where \(G_i \equiv 1/N\) everywhere), so the strategic correction is invisible until positions have started to separate.

Parameters:

  • positions (numpy.ndarray) – Agent positions, shape (N, L).

  • grid (numpy.ndarray) – Trait points, shape (K, L).

  • cov (numpy.ndarray) – Shared MV-Gaussian covariance \(\Sigma\), shape (L, L).

  • eps (float) – Tiny floor for numerical stability when all \(G_i(1-G_i)\) at some trait approach zero (e.g. one agent has \(G_i \to 1\) and the rest have \(G_i \to 0\)); falls back to uniform routing at that trait.

Returns:

Strategic routing matrix P with P[i, k] the strategic routing probability of agent i at trait b_k. Shape (N, K); P.sum(axis=0) is identically one.

Return type:

numpy.ndarray

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.top_k_allocation_weights(G, top_k)[source]¶

Top-\(k\) sparsified, per-query renormalised allocation weights.

Used by the soft (dense) routing mode of the closed loop. Whereas hard routing samples a single agent per query from \(G_i(\mathbf{x}, b)\), soft routing trains every agent on the query with a per-example loss weight equal to its (renormalised) allocation share. To cap the \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) blow-up in SFT compute, only the top_k most-allocated agents per query are kept; their weights are renormalised so each query column sums to one (mass per query is conserved).

Setting top_k == 1 recovers a deterministic hard assignment (one agent per query at unit weight — the \(\arg\max_i G_i\) winner); top_k >= N keeps the full dense allocation.

Parameters:

  • G (numpy.ndarray) – Allocation matrix \(G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k)\), shape (N, K). Columns are expected to sum to one across agents (as returned by allocation_weights()) but this is not required — the output is renormalised regardless.

  • top_k (int) – Number of highest-allocation agents to retain per query. Must satisfy top_k >= 1.

Returns:

Sparsified weight matrix W with the same shape as G; each column has at most top_k non-zero entries and sums to one (except an all-zero query column, which is left at zero). Shape (N, K).

Return type:

numpy.ndarray

Raises:

ValueError – If top_k < 1 or G is not 2-D.

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.group_allocation_weights(G, group_index, n_groups)[source]¶

Sum per-agent allocation rows into per-group rows.

\[G_p(\mathbf{x}, b) \;=\; \sum_{i \in p} G_i(\mathbf{x}, b)\]

Used by soft routing over merge groups: when a group’s members are co-located at one shared position and every group has the same size, the summed share equals the allocation \(G_p\) of a single agent placed at that shared position in the n_groups-agent game (the common member count cancels in the numerator and denominator of eqn. 1). With unequal group sizes the sum is still the group’s total share of the query, but it is no longer the allocation of an equivalent single agent.

Columns of the result sum to one whenever the columns of G do.

Parameters:

  • G (numpy.ndarray) – Allocation matrix \(G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k)\), shape (N, K), as returned by allocation_weights().

  • group_index (numpy.ndarray) – Group id per agent row, shape (N,), with values in [0, n_groups).

  • n_groups (int) – Number of groups \(P\).

Returns:

Group allocation matrix, shape (P, K).

Return type:

numpy.ndarray

Raises:

ValueError – If G is not 2-D, group_index does not have one entry per agent row, n_groups < 1, or any group id lies outside [0, n_groups).

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.empirical_utility(positions, query_coords, cov)[source]¶

Empirical-pool utility \(\hat u_i = \frac{1}{M}\sum_m G_i(\mathbf{x}, b^\ast_m)\).

Whereas expected_utilities() evaluates \(u_i = \sum_k B_\text{KDE}(b_k)\, G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k)\) against the KDE-smoothed resource density on a discretised grid, this function averages \(G_i\) against the actual embedded query corpus, treating each query as a unit-mass sample from the empirical resource distribution. The two coincide in the limit of (large corpus) ∩ (fine grid) ∩ (small KDE bandwidth); they can disagree noticeably for small corpora, coarse grids, or wide Scott’s-rule bandwidths.

The empirical-pool utility is what the proportional routing mechanism actually consumes: for a batch of \(M\) queries IID from the pool,

\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{N_i}{M}\right] \;=\; \hat u_i(\mathbf{x}),\]

where \(N_i\) is the count of queries routed to agent \(i\) under policy='proportional'.

Parameters:

  • positions (numpy.ndarray) – Agent positions, shape (N, L).

  • query_coords (numpy.ndarray) – Embedded query coordinates in trait space, shape (M, L). Typically obtained via trait_space.project(list_of_query_strings).

  • cov (numpy.ndarray) – Shared MV-Gaussian covariance \(\Sigma\), shape (L, L).

Returns:

Per-agent empirical utility, shape (N,). Sums to one.

Return type:

numpy.ndarray

Raises:

ValueError – If query_coords is empty.

infl_ens.inflgame.router.allocation.utility_gradient(positions, grid, weights, cov)[source]¶

Closed-form gradient \(\nabla_{x_i} u_i(\mathbf{x})\).

Using

\[\nabla_{x_i} \log f_i \;=\; -\Sigma^{-1}(x_i - b), \quad \nabla_{x_i} G_i \;=\; G_i\,(1 - G_i)\, \nabla_{x_i} \log f_i,\]

we have

\[\nabla_{x_i} u_i \;=\; \sum_k B(b_k)\, G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k)\,(1 - G_i(\mathbf{x}, b_k))\, \big(-\Sigma^{-1}(x_i - b_k)\big).\]

Note this is the gradient of only player i’s own utility with respect to their own position — what the gradient-ascent dynamics \(\nabla_t x_i = \nabla_{x_i} u_i\) consume.

Parameters:

  • positions (numpy.ndarray) – Agent positions, shape (N, L).

  • grid (numpy.ndarray) – Trait points, shape (K, L).

  • weights (numpy.ndarray) – Resource weights \(B(b_k)\), shape (K,).

  • cov (numpy.ndarray) – Shared covariance \(\Sigma\), shape (L, L).

Returns:

Stacked gradient matrix, shape (N, L); row i is \(\nabla_{x_i} u_i\).

Return type:

numpy.ndarray
